ety.text: Latin cuneusder. Old French coinbor. Middle English coyn English coin From Middle English coyn, from Old French coigne (“wedge, cornerstone, die for stamping”), from Latin cuneus (“wedge”). Doublet of coign and cuneus. See also quoin (“cornerstone”). Displaced Middle English mynt, from Old English mynet (whence modern English mint), which was derived from Latin monēta.

senses.d: A piece of currency, usually metallic and in the shape of a disc, but sometimes polygonal, or with a hole in the middle.
ex: ...the coins were of all countries and sizes - doubloons, and louis d'ors, and guineas, and pieces of eight...

senses.d: A token used in a special establishment like a casino.
That which serves for payment or recompense.
ex: The loss of every present advantage to flesh and blood is repaid in a nobler coin.

senses.d: Something in broad circulation or use.
Money in general, not limited to coins.
ex: She spent some serious coin on that car!
Boy toy named Troy, used to live in Detroit, big dope dealer money he was getting some coin.

senses.d: One of the suits of minor arcana in tarot, or a card of that suit.
A corner or external angle.
A small circular slice of food.
ex: For munchies try deep-fried jalapeño coins, jumbo Buffalo wings, and hush puppies with a sweet edge.
Spread out four bread and butter pickle coins on top, and sprinkle with onion.

senses.d: To make of a definite fineness, and convert into coins, as a mass of metal.
ex: to coin silver dollars
to coin a medal

senses.d: To make or fabricate (especially a word or phrase).
ex: Over the last century the advance in science has led to many new words being coined.
Not fearing outward force: So ſhall my Lungs / Coine words till their decay, againſt thoſe Meazels

senses.d: To acquire rapidly, as money; to make.

From Middle English coilen, from Old French coillir, cuillir (“to gather, pluck, pick, cull”) (modern French cueillir), from Latin colligō (“to gather together”), past participle collectus, from com- (“together”) + legō (“to gather”); compare legend. Doublet of cull.

senses.d: Something wound in the form of a helix or spiral.
ex: the sinuous coils of a snake
The wild grapevines that twisted their coils or tendrils from tree to tree.

senses.d: Any intrauterine device for contraception (originally coil-shaped).
ex: ‘I’m gonna go on the pill and get fitted for a coil. I don’t wanna be pregnant. Ever. Again!’

senses.d: A coil of electrically conductive wire through which electricity can flow.
A cylinder of clay.
Entanglement; perplexity.
ex:
What trifling coil do we mortals keep;
Wake, eat, and drink, evacuate, and sleep.

senses.d: To wind or reel e.g. a wire or rope into regular rings, often around a centerpiece.
ex: A simple transformer can be made by coiling two pieces of insulated copper wire around an iron heart.

senses.d: To wind into loops (roughly) around a common center.
ex: The sailor coiled the free end of the hawser on the pier.

senses.d: To wind cylindrically or spirally.
ex: to coil a rope when not in use
The snake coiled itself before springing.

senses.d: To build a pot (etc) with clay coils.
To encircle and hold with, or as if with, coils.
ex:
a. 1757, Thomas Edwards, sonnet to Mr. Nathanael Mason
Pleasure coil thee in her dangerous snare

senses.d: A noise, tumult, bustle, or turmoil.
ex: this great Savage desired also to see him. A great coyle there was to set him forward.
His liver demanded activity, namely, a quarrel, and what a coil this was!

senses.d: A wad of cash.

grp.label: coil of electrically conductive wire through which electricity can flow — see also inductor

chain.g: A thing that is coiled, twisted, or wound.

Borrowed from Latin helīcem, from Ancient Greek ἕλῑξ (hélīx, “spiral”).
Probably from Latin balbus because of the noise it made.

chain.g: serpentine; of or pertaining to a serpent or snake

pt:enrolar.gl: to curl or coil (up), to wrap around

ety.text: From French coïncider, from Medieval Latin coincidere, from con- + incidere, from in- (“into, to”) + cadere (“to fall, fall down, drop”).

senses.d: To occupy exactly the same space.
ex: The two squares coincide nicely.

senses.d: To occur at the same time.
ex: The conference will coincide with his vacation.

senses.d: To correspond, concur, or agree.
ex: Our ideas coincide, except in certain areas.

grp.label: to occupy exactly the same space
to occur at the same time

ety.text: Latin coinciderebor. Spanish coincidir Borrowed from Latin coincidere.
From French coïncider, from Latin coincidere. By surface analysis, co- + incidir.
From Middle French coincidence (French coïncidence). By surface analysis, coincide + -ence.

senses.d: The property of being coincident, occurring at the same time or place.
The appearance of a meaningful connection between events when there is none.
ex: That the two writers were born and died on the same day is just a coincidence, although there are many conspiracy theories about it.
It is sheer coincidence that the cartoon resembles the local politician.

senses.d: A coincidence point.
A fixed point of a correspondence; a point of a variety corresponding to itself under a correspondence.

grp.label: of objects, property of being coincident
state of events appearing to be connected when they are not

ety.text: Medieval Latin coincidentiabor. French coïncidence Borrowed from Medieval Latin coincidentia.
From casual + -idad; cognate with Galician casualidade.
